case_name: CASE OF MLADINA D.D. LJUBLJANA v. SLOVENIA (No. 2)

assessment.Existence of an interference: The measures imposed on the applicant company — an obligation to publish an apology and judgment and, later, to pay EUR 3,000 in compensation — clearly amounted to an interference with its freedom of expression under Article 10 (see paragraphs 17, 25 and 30). That interference was based on domestic civil-law provisions protecting personality rights and reputation (see paragraphs 32-33) and pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the rights of others, in particular B.G.'s honour and reputation in connection with the publication of the family photographs (see paragraphs 13, 18 and 24). The central issue is therefore whether the interference was 'necessary in a democratic society'.

assessment.Applicable principles under Article 10: Where expression concerns both public-interest reporting and possible harm to reputation or private life, the Court usually examines whether domestic courts balanced the competing interests using the established criteria: contribution to a debate of general interest, notoriety of the person concerned, prior conduct, content, form and consequences of the publication, and the circumstances in which photographs were taken (see nos. 39954/08, 40660/08, 60641/08, 40454/07). Political speech and satire attract a high level of protection, especially where they concern a prominent opposition politician (see paragraphs 5, 8 and 20). However, that protection is not unlimited, particularly when expression shifts from criticism of political conduct to a highly intrusive visual association affecting family life and children (see paragraphs 9, 18, 23 and 24).

assessment.Contribution to a debate of public inter: The impugned publication formed part of an ongoing public controversy. Before Mladina published the satirical piece, there had already been a public debate after D.S. had posted a photograph comparing B.G. with Joseph Goebbels (see paragraph 6). The editor-in-chief's editorial in the same issue discussed alleged similarities in propaganda methods between the SDS and the Nazi model, and the applicant company maintained throughout the proceedings that its aim was to criticise B.G.'s political methods and his use of family imagery for political gain (see paragraphs 7, 12 and 14). This strongly supports the applicant company's Article 10 claim: the publication was not wholly devoid of public-interest content, and B.G. was unquestionably a public figure who had to display a greater degree of tolerance toward criticism (see paragraphs 5 and 15).

assessment.Private-life weight of the visual compar: The decisive difficulty for the applicant company lies in the visual element. The article in the satirical section did not merely use harsh language about a politician; it placed side by side Joseph Goebbels' family photograph and a photograph of B.G. with his wife and three young children, in an identical format and similar composition (see paragraphs 8-10). The domestic courts accepted that the texts could be understood as political criticism, yet they distinguished the photographs because images may affect personal rights more intensely than words and because the visual message targeted B.G. not only as a politician but also as a father (see paragraphs 18, 20, 23 and 24). That assessment appears persuasive. Even though the photo of B.G.'s family had been taken at a public religious event and his family had previously been exposed to the media (see paragraphs 10 and 15), prior exposure could not reasonably be taken as consent to a later comparison between his family and the family of a leading Nazi figure (see paragraph 24). The fact that the children appeared to be under ten years old further strengthens the private-life side of the balance (see paragraph 9).

assessment.Context, satire and the perspective of t: The applicant company argued that the impugned piece had to be read together with the editorial and subsequent articles clarifying that only political methods were being compared (see paragraphs 14 and 21). Yet the Higher Court, Supreme Court and Constitutional Court all found that the satirical item in 'Mladinamit' had a sufficiently autonomous impact and that the average reader might see the photographs without integrating the editorial's nuance, especially since the photographs were published in a separate section (see paragraphs 18, 20, 23 and 24). The Court generally gives substantial weight to the immediate effect of photographs and headlines. Here, the short satirical text ('Sieg!') did not neutralise the visual message; rather, it amplified the provocation (see paragraph 8). It was therefore open to the domestic courts to find that the publication went beyond robust political satire and created a shocking association between two families, not merely two political styles (see paragraphs 20, 23 and 24).

assessment.Quality of the domestic balancing exerci: This is not a case where the national courts ignored the public-interest dimension or the applicant company's journalistic freedom. On the contrary, the first-instance court initially dismissed the claim on Article 10-oriented grounds (see paragraph 15), and the higher courts later accepted that the texts themselves had not unlawfully damaged B.G.'s reputation (see paragraph 18). The later judgments carefully narrowed the interference to the publication and comparison of the family photographs. They expressly considered the satirical nature of the section, B.G.'s status as a politician, the public nature of the event where the photograph was taken, his prior willingness to expose his family, and the wider political debate surrounding comparisons with Goebbels (see paragraphs 20, 23, 24 and 27). They nonetheless concluded that the visual comparison crossed the line. Given that the domestic courts applied criteria closely aligned with the Court's case-law in photo-publication cases (see nos. 39954/08, 40660/08, 60641/08, 40454/07), the Strasbourg Court would likely require strong reasons to depart from that assessment; such reasons do not clearly emerge from the facts.

assessment.Proportionality of the sanctions: The sanctions imposed were relatively moderate. The applicant company was ordered to publish an apology and, after remittal and review, to pay EUR 3,000 rather than the much larger sum initially claimed by B.G. (see paragraphs 13, 17, 25 and 30). The domestic courts explicitly addressed the need to avoid a chilling effect on journalism and reduced the compensation accordingly (see paragraphs 27 and 30). There was no ban on further reporting about B.G. or the underlying political controversy. In these circumstances, the penalty appears proportionate to the narrow aspect of the publication found unlawful.

assessment.Overall conclusion: Although the impugned publication arose in the context of political debate and satire, the decisive element is that the applicant company chose to convey its criticism through a side-by-side comparison of B.G.'s family, including small children, with the family of Joseph Goebbels (see paragraphs 8-10). The domestic courts did not sanction the applicant company for criticising B.G.'s politics as such; they sanctioned only the visual comparison involving his family, after a detailed balancing exercise consistent with Article 10 principles (see paragraphs 18, 20, 23, 24 and 30). In light of the special weight of the family and children's interests and the limited nature of the sanctions, the interference would likely be regarded as necessary in a democratic society. Therefore, a finding of no violation of Article 10 is the more likely outcome.
